cim: A statement from LPM on artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: A statement from LPM on artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
A statement from Kenya Young, President & CEO of LPM:

Yesterday, Louisville Public Media published a statement of our practices on how we are addressing the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). It explains how we use AI and how we don't, and it outlines the standards and guiding principles behind that use.

Why now? Because AI is moving fast, people are asking questions, and the public deserves to know where we stand. Trust is what we aspire to build every day.

We are living in a moment when you have to wonder whether the video in your feed really happened, whether the voice on a phone call belongs to a human and whether the comment under a story came from a bot. Media companies across the country are cutting staff, and some have tied those cuts directly to their increased use of AI. Data centers are going up in communities, particularly here in Kentucky, for better or for worse depending on whom you ask.

At the same time, AI is undoubtedly changing how people work and navigate their days, helping them move faster, find information quicker and solve problems that once took days, weeks and even months.

A generation ago, the internet changed the media landscape, in some ways for the better and in others for the worse. It upended newsrooms around the world, and many did not survive. AI is the next technology of that scale.

So how is LPM addressing these complexities, and how is it showing up in what you hear, see and read?

LPM has been watching closely, and we have been planning for this evolving landscape. AI is part of our new three-year strategic plan, under our priority of Digital Transformation and Adaptability. In the plan's words, LPM will "adopt AI tools, with clear ethical standards, that increase efficiency and responsiveness, freeing staff capacity for higher-value work."

What does that mean? As the world evolves, LPM must evolve too, across every platform where you find us: on air, online, on your phone and in person. And yes, that includes evolving alongside AI. In practice, that means using tools that take on routine tasks so our people have more time for what matters most: reporting, curating music and being out in the community. When we do use AI, we will apply the same professional standards and ethics that guide everything we do.

LPM is in the beginning stages of adapting to AI. We are exploring, experimenting and yes, in some cases, already using AI tools for work behind the scenes. That includes tasks like transcription, research and data analysis. But anything we use AI for is reviewed and checked by a person.

We use AI on the back end, where it saves time, so our people can spend more of their time on the front end: in the community, reporting, curating and creating.

We don't see AI as a quick fix or a way to cut corners. We engage with it, question it and challenge it. We take the wins when it saves us time, but accuracy always comes first. Whatever AI helps with, our staff own the final result.

We don't use AI to write our stories. Our journalists report for, about and in the community, and that will not change. They source our stories, conduct the interviews and write the news.

We don't use AI to choose the music you hear, and we don't play AI-generated music on air. Our hosts and music staff decide what plays on WFPK and WUOL.

We will not use AI to replicate anyone's voice or to alter real audio, photos or video.

Technology companies, including AI companies, have invested heavily in journalism and media in recent years. LPM has received support from some of them, including the Google News Initiative and the OpenAI Foundation's People-First AI Fund.

As our ethics and independence policy states, "There is no connection between our funding and editorial decisions. By virtue of their contributions, members, businesses and donors to LPM have no direct access to the newsroom, programming or those who make content decisions."

That holds for technology companies, too. Their support comes with no influence over what news we cover or what music we play, and no commitment to any company's products.

As LPM continues to evolve, three things remain true:

The most important theme in our strategic plan is trust. We know trust can't be asked for. It has to be earned, every day – with every concerto on WUOL, every new artist on WFPK and every local story on WFPL. That will not change.

President and CEOLouisville Public Media
